pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Dinosaur Sizes (ages 5–7): dinosaurs came in a huge range of sizes — some as tall as a house or as long as a bus, others as small as a chicken — and we understand their size by comparing them to familiar things.
• Standards — UK (DfE): supports KS1 maths 'Measurement' (compare lengths/heights using longer/shorter, taller/shorter) and science 'working scientifically' (compare and describe); dinosaurs are the engaging context for non-standard size comparison.
• Standards — US (NGSS/CCSS-M): aligns with K–1 measurement/comparison (describe and compare measurable attributes; directly compare two objects); no dino-specific PE.
• Operational details — The concept is COMPARISON, not absolute numbers: anchor size to familiar referents (child, bus, house, chicken) using comparative language (taller than, longer than, heavier than). Crucially bust the 'all dinosaurs were huge' idea — include a chicken-sized dinosaur alongside a giant so the RANGE is felt. Avoid abstract metres/tonnes; use body-scale and everyday-object scale. Optionally note the biggest were plant-eating long-necks and some meat-eaters were small.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~5): says some dinosaurs were very big and some were small. Tier B (~6): compares a dinosaur to a familiar object ('taller than a bus'). Tier C (~7): orders several dinosaurs by size and uses comparative language, recognising dinosaurs ranged from chicken-sized to house-sized.
bestPractices: Always compare to a FAMILIAR referent (child, bus, house, chicken) rather than abstract units — body/object scale is how young children grasp size.
Deliberately include a tiny dinosaur next to a giant so the RANGE (not just bigness) is the takeaway.
Use rich comparative language consistently: taller than / longer than / heavier than / smaller than.
Let children physically or visually line up figures to order them, making comparison an action.
Relate to their own height ('this one's leg is taller than your whole class standing on each other') to make scale visceral.
keyRepresentations: Silhouette scale line-ups: dinosaur beside a person, bus, house, and chicken.
An order-by-size strip from smallest (chicken-sized) to largest (long-neck giant).
A 'stand next to it' overlay putting a child figure beside each dinosaur.
Comparative-word cards (taller/longer/heavier) attached to each comparison.
commonMisconceptions: 'All dinosaurs were enormous' — many were small; some were chicken- or turkey-sized.
'The scariest/meat-eaters were the biggest' — the very largest were plant-eating long-necks; some carnivores were tiny.
'Dinosaurs were all bigger than any animal today' — small dinosaurs were the size of familiar small animals.
'Bigger dinosaur means it lived more recently / is more advanced' — size is not a timeline.
'Pictures show real relative size' when objects aren't drawn to a common scale — fair comparison needs the same scale.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach that dinosaurs came in a huge RANGE of sizes — some as tall as a house or long as a bus, others as small as a chicken — by comparing dinosaurs to familiar referents (a child, a bus, a house, a chicken) using comparative language (taller than, longer than, heavier than, smaller than). The central insight is the range itself, not absolute metres or tonnes, so always pair a giant with a tiny dinosaur. Keep comparisons at a shared scale so they are fair.

activities.title: Compare dinosaurs to your own world (scale stage)
feedback: If a child expects every dinosaur to be giant, follow the house-tall sauropod immediately with the chicken-sized Compsognathus so the contrast lands.
When a comparison is stated, echo it back with the comparative word: 'Yes — taller than the house.'
If scale seems abstract, use the personal referent: 'This leg is taller than you.'
Confirm the key takeaway: some dinosaurs were enormous AND some were tiny — both are real dinosaurs.
activities.rationale: Young children grasp size through body- and object-scale comparison rather than abstract units; placing a dinosaur beside a familiar referent and pairing a giant with a tiny species makes the real size range concrete. Optional interactions — a movable familiar-object tray, an auto comparative caption, and a 'stand next to it' child avatar — make the comparison mechanism concrete without being mandatory, and their comparative efficacy is not established here.
sourceClaims: Dinosaurs spanned an enormous size range — the largest sauropods (e.g. Brachiosaurus, Argentinosaurus) were among the biggest land animals ever, while small theropods such as Compsognathus were roughly the size of a chicken/turkey.
learnerActions: Place a chosen familiar object on a comparison stage: yourself (a child figure), a bus, a house, and a chicken.

Bring a dinosaur alongside the chosen object at the same shared scale and look at how they compare — e.g. Brachiosaurus reaching past the roof of a house, Compsognathus barely bigger than the chicken.
Say or complete a comparison out loud: 'Brachiosaurus is taller than the house', 'Compsognathus is smaller than a big dog'.
Use a 'stand next to it' option to drop a small version of yourself beside each dinosaur and say how it compares to you ('its leg is taller than me!').
Deliberately compare a giant and a tiny dinosaur one after the other so you feel the contrast.
activities.intendedInsight: Dinosaurs ranged from chicken-sized to house-sized; not all were huge. Size is a relation you understand by comparing to familiar things at the same scale.

activities.title: Order dinosaurs from smallest to biggest
feedback: If the order is wrong, compare just two at a time: 'Which of these two is longer?' and rebuild from there.
Praise correct use of comparative language, not just correct placement.
If a child places them all as 'big', revisit the smallest example and compare it to the chicken.
activities.rationale: Making comparison an action — physically or visually lining figures up — helps children feel the spread and practise ordering. An order-by-size rail that snaps into place when correct is one optional way to give immediate feedback; this is a proposed scaffold, not a validated method.
learnerActions: Take a jumbled set of several dinosaurs (including a chicken-sized one and a long-necked giant) and arrange them in a line from shortest to longest (smallest to largest by length).
Say which is smallest and which is largest, and name one of each if you can (e.g. Compsognathus small, Brachiosaurus large).
Attach or say a comparative word for each neighbouring pair (this one is longer than that one).
activities.intendedInsight: Dinosaurs can be ordered by size, and the full spread runs from tiny to gigantic.

activities.title: To-scale line-up poster (scaffold)
feedback: If a child thinks every dinosaur is huge, point to the chicken-sized one on the same poster.
Reinforce that the comparison is fair only because everything is drawn to the same scale.
activities.rationale: A pre-drawn to-scale line-up presents comparison and the size range clearly in one view. It is a scaffold: the referents and ordering are fixed, so the child cannot test their own comparisons or build the order themselves — use it alongside hands-on ordering.
sourceClaims: Dinosaurs spanned an enormous size range — the largest sauropods (e.g. Brachiosaurus, Argentinosaurus) were among the biggest land animals ever, while small theropods such as Compsognathus were roughly the size of a chicken/turkey.
learnerActions: Look at a poster where dinosaurs are drawn beside a bus, a house, and a child at the same shared scale.
Point to each dinosaur and read or say its comparison: 'as tall as a house', 'as small as a chicken'.
Find the biggest and the smallest on the poster and describe the difference.
activities.intendedInsight: A fair comparison uses a common scale, and a single picture can show the full range at once.

activities.title: Check the 'all dinosaurs were giant' idea
feedback: Full understanding: disagrees with the friend, gives a named giant AND a named tiny example, and uses comparison words.
If the child agrees all were giant: show paired examples — a house-tall sauropod beside a chicken-sized Compsognathus.
If the child says a tiny one isn't a real dinosaur: being a dinosaur is about the kind of animal, not its size.
If the child says all dinosaurs beat every modern animal: a blue whale today is bigger than most dinosaurs.
activities.rationale: A two-tier diagnostic surfaces the 'all dinosaurs were huge' misconception and the related errors that small species 'don't count' or that all dinosaurs exceeded modern animals. Requiring both a large and a small named example discriminates genuine understanding of the range from agreement with the giant stereotype.
sourceClaims: Dinosaurs spanned an enormous size range — the largest sauropods (e.g. Brachiosaurus, Argentinosaurus) were among the biggest land animals ever, while small theropods such as Compsognathus were roughly the size of a chicken/turkey.
learnerActions: Respond to a friend who says: 'ALL dinosaurs were gigantic — as big as a house or bigger. A dinosaur the size of a chicken couldn't be a real dinosaur.' Agree or disagree, and explain.
Name one really big dinosaur and one really small dinosaur.
Answer: Was every dinosaur bigger than an elephant? What about a blue whale living today?
Finish: 'Brachiosaurus was ___ than a bus; Compsognathus was ___ than a big dog.'
activities.intendedInsight: Dinosaurs came in a huge range of sizes; a small, chicken-sized dinosaur is still a real dinosaur, and some living animals (like a blue whale) are bigger than most dinosaurs.

constraints: Compare to a FAMILIAR referent (child, bus, house, chicken), not abstract metres or tonnes — body/object scale is how young children grasp size.
Always include a tiny dinosaur next to a giant so RANGE, not just bigness, is the takeaway.
Comparisons are fair only at a common scale; if objects aren't drawn to the same scale the picture can mislead.
The to-scale poster is a scaffold: it fixes the referents and ordering, so pair it with hands-on ordering and personal 'how does this compare to me?' comparison.

Multiple-choice or sequence checks can verify comparison and ordering but do not by themselves give the felt, manipulable scale experience; use them to assess alongside, rather than as the sole, teaching.
This is a comparison concept, not a timeline: bigger does not mean more recent or more advanced; the largest were plant-eating long-necks while some meat-eaters were small.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The single cited source is marked verified:false in the row; the chicken/turkey size comparison for Compsognathus and the 'among the biggest land animals' claim for the named sauropods are reported from NHM/Smithsonian but not independently re-checked here.
Comparative physical facts (e.g. a blue whale is bigger than most dinosaurs) are used at an age-appropriate level; broadly accepted but not re-verified against sources in this rewrite.

The non-preferred 3D and conversation entries carried universal-sounding claims ('true 3D depth isn't required', 'dialogue cannot deliver the comparison'); these were softened to scoped affordance/limit statements (a 2D shared-scale stage shows height/length comparison without depth; dialogue can state facts but a talk/sort does not itself produce side-by-side visual comparison) rather than propagated as laws.

The ordering activity's sourceClaims were set to [] because the cited claim supports the size-range facts, not the proposed 'ordering as an action' teaching method. The size-range claim is retained on activities whose content directly presents or depends on that factual range (scale stage, poster, diagnostic).

probeDeeper: Can you name one really big dinosaur and one really small dinosaur?
Was every dinosaur bigger than an elephant? What about a blue whale living today?
Finish these: Brachiosaurus was ___ than a bus; Compsognathus was ___ than a dog.
assess.correctAnswer: Disagree. Dinosaurs came in a huge RANGE of sizes: some were enormous (Brachiosaurus, taller than a house), but others were tiny — as small as a chicken (like Compsognathus). A small dinosaur is still a real dinosaur, so 'all dinosaurs were gigantic' is wrong.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the range with paired examples — a house-tall sauropod beside a chicken-sized Compsognathus; size varied enormously.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — every dinosaur was huge, house-sized or bigger.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Agrees with the friend; denies small dinosaurs existed.

errorPatterns.pattern: A small, chicken-sized dinosaur isn't a real dinosaur.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confirm small dinosaurs are fully dinosaurs; being a dinosaur is about the kind of animal, not its size.
errorPatterns.distractor: A chicken-sized one is too small to be a real dinosaur.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Excludes small species from being dinosaurs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Dinosaurs were all bigger than every animal alive today.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare to today — a blue whale is bigger than most dinosaurs; and many dinosaurs were small.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims all dinosaurs exceeded modern animals in size.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks all dinosaurs were giant, or that small ones don't count as dinosaurs.
responseLevels.full: Describes a real size range with a named large and small example and comparison words, and accepts small dinosaurs as genuine dinosaurs.
responseLevels.partial: Knows some were big and some smaller but can't give a clear small example or use comparison language.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Your friend says 'ALL dinosaurs were gigantic — as big as a house or bigger. A dinosaur the size of a chicken couldn't be a real dinosaur.' Do you agree? Explain what the range of dinosaur sizes was really like.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the 'all dinosaurs were giant' image agrees with the friend and rejects small dinosaurs. Only a child who knows the size range disagrees and can supply both a giant and a tiny named example — which the tier-two 'what was the range really like' requires.
